title: Patacara
hook: she loses husband, children and parents in one day and runs wild; the Buddha says, sister, recover your mind

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mustard seed, and every house had known death. Your line: no house is untouched.

This week is hard stories, and today's is the hardest to hear, so breathe as you listen. Some overwhelm isn't one blow but many, landing before you've gotten up from the last. The mind just can't hold any more. Patacara was the daughter of a wealthy family in Savatthi. She fell in love with a servant in her parents' house and ran away with him, and they lived poor, far from her family. Pregnant with their second child, she set out with her husband and little son to walk home to her parents. And a storm came.
screen: `BREATHE AS YOU LISTEN.` → `NOT ONE BLOW, BUT MANY.` → `A WALK HOME, AND A STORM.`

segments.voice: The story comes from the commentaries; i'll tell it plainly and briefly. In the storm, she gives birth by the road. Her husband goes to find branches for shelter, a snake bites him, and he dies. In the morning, with a newborn and a toddler, she reaches a river swollen with rain. She carries the baby across first, lays him on the far bank, and turns back for her older son. A hawk swoops toward the baby. She waves and shouts to scare it off, and her little boy, on the other bank, thinks she's calling him, steps into the river, and is swept away. The hawk takes the baby. At Savatthi a traveler tells her that in the night's storm her parents' house fell, killing her mother, father and brother. She can see the smoke of their cremation. Her mind breaks. She runs through the streets, her clothes falling away, and people throw dirt at her and chase her off. She runs into the grove where the Buddha is teaching. People try to stop her. He says, let her come. When she's near, he says: sister, recover your mind. Sister. Not madwoman. Not sinner. She comes back to herself. Someone throws her a cloak. She sits at his feet and tells him everything. He listens. He doesn't tell her it didn't happen. He tells her that across the long round of lives, the tears shed for loved ones are more than the water in the oceans. She isn't alone in it. Patacara became a nun, and in time a teacher of other women. Her verses survive in the Therigatha, beside verses from women who came to her grieving.
screen: `A STORM, A SNAKE, A RIVER.` · `SHE RUNS WILD THROUGH THE CITY.` · `SISTER, RECOVER YOUR MIND.` · `A TEACHER OF WOMEN WHO LOST.` · then, large: `RECOVER YOUR MIND.`

segments.voice: Put one hand on your chest; breathe in for four, hold a moment, and breathe out for six, the out-breath always longer. If you like, let a word ride on it, the way Patacara heard one word: sister. Learned while calm, the way back is there when you're overwhelmed.
Patacara. The woman who lost everyone in a day, heard the words, sister, recover your mind, and became a teacher of women.
Your line: recover your mind. The way back can start with one word. That's seventy-six.

howItsDone: Buddhists remember Patacara as a great nun and teacher of women, honored for her mastery of the monastic discipline, and her verses and those of her students are preserved in the Therigatha.

original.note: Pali: sister. What the Buddha called Patacara as she came toward him.

trapdoor: what you thought: a tragedy with a happy ending tacked on.
what it means: a woman whose mind broke under grief, met with one kind word, who became a teacher of other grieving women.
what a scholar hears: Dhammapada commentary on verse 113 and the Therigatha commentary; her verses are Therigatha 112–116; 'recover your mind' renders satim patilabha: get back your presence of mind.
recall: the chief disciple known for his wisdom
burning, as with greed, hate and delusion

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 15.3 (tears more than the four oceans)

notes: Sensitive: deaths of a husband, two children and parents. Told plainly and briefly; Keeper to confirm tone and whether any detail (people throwing dirt) should be cut.
The story is commentarial; details (snake bite, the Aciravati river, the hawk, the collapsed house) follow the Dhammapada commentary. Confirm.
The tears-and-oceans teaching attributed to the Buddha's words to her follows the commentary, which draws on the Assu Sutta (SN 15.3). Confirm.
'Recover your mind' = satim patilabha, bhagini (commentary). Confirm Pali.
Patacara as expert in Vinaya and teacher of many women (Thig 117–121 are her students' verses; later tradition mentions 500). Confirm.
